content: Drug Susceptibility Testing (DST) for tuberculosis (TB) is conducted using both first-line drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and streptomycin) and second-line drugs (fluoroquinolones and injectables). These tests are performed using either liquid or solid media. Additional diagnostic tools include electrocardiograms (ECG), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) tests, fine needle biopsies (for children), full blood counts (including red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets), gastric lavage (for children), random blood sugar (RBS) tests, HIV confirmatory and rapid tests, interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA), lactic acid tests, and lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assays (LF-LAM) for TB antigen detection. Other tests include lipase levels, line probe assays (LPA) for first-line and second-line drugs, Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) microscopy, sputum induction, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels, total white blood cell counts, tuberculin skin tests (TST), and chest X-rays. Molecular diagnostic tools like Xpert® MTB/RIF are also utilized. Community-based TB interventions include diagnostic visits, screening visits, treatment visits, vaccination campaigns (e.g., BCG vaccination), and follow-up tracing through phone calls. Patient support is provided during both diagnosis and treatment phases. The costing guidelines for TB interventions involve collecting data from 15–25 TB service providers, including health facilities and laboratories, over 1–3 days per site. The data collection process examines financial and service records, lists all rooms and equipment used for TB services, and interviews staff about their time allocation. Local prices for salaries, supplies, and equipment are also gathered. The process is piloted at two sites before detailed costing is conducted at five sites. Data is entered electronically using mobile devices. The study team is led by a principal investigator (PI) and a local PI, supported by at least two research assistants and a local consultant or member of the National TB Programme (NTP) in a supervisory role. Research assistants collect data from 15–25 facilities over a year, working full-time. The NTP collaborates with the study team to identify local consultants, design the study protocol, train data collectors, facilitate access to providers, and support local ethics submissions. The NTP also aids in disseminating findings and translating research into policy. They liaise with stakeholders, manage funding, and lead the analysis and dissemination of results. Research assistants are trained in costing techniques and data collection tools, conduct interviews, analyze records, and manage field data. They must have strong social and communication skills and be proficient in technology if online tools are used. A technical advisory group provides input on statistical, epidemiological, and health economics aspects of the study. This group collaborates during protocol design and analysis phases and may include international experts. Data collected will be shared in an open-access repository to enable generalization to other settings. Case studies illustrate the workflow in TB clinics and laboratories. For example, a Kenyan clinic in a peri-urban area provides TB services in a separate room, with patients receiving weekly pre-packaged anti-TB medications. Community health workers conduct home visits for treatment observation. In Romania, a hospital laboratory performs Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) and Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) tests, with detailed interviews conducted to determine costs for consumables, reagents, and equipment. Overhead costs are calculated based on laboratory space and annual test volumes.
